sets.t: Head-to-Toe Clinical Assessment Guide: Essay questions

qs.q: What follow-up action is required after completing a comprehensive head-to-toe clinical assessment and identifying significant patient abnormalities?
qs.e: Assessment follow-up explicitly includes notifying the physician of identified abnormalities. Immediate discharge or stopping documentation would endanger patient safety.

faq.a: Check for malaria (rapid test) and hepatitis B; examine for hemolysis signs and order CBC and bilirubin.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient is febrile with jaundice?

faq.a: Ascites gives a dull area that shifts when the patient turns; bowel sounds are tympanic and do not shift.
faq.q: How do I differentiate ascites from a large bowel loop on percussion?

faq.a: NSAIDs can mask fever and worsen renal function; prioritize antitubercular therapy and supportive care.
faq.q: Why avoid non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs in a patient with suspected TB pleuritis?

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect severe malaria in a febrile patient? — Periodic chills, pallor, splenomegaly, high parasite count on rapid test.
A patient presents with dyspnoea, peripheral edema and a raised JVP. How do you distinguish heart failure from severe anemia? — Look for pulmonary crackles, displaced apex, and normal JVP in anemia.
If the rapid malaria test is negative but suspicion remains high, what is your next step? — Obtain thick and thin blood smears; start empirical artesunate if critically ill.
Which WHO danger signs in a child with fever mandate immediate referral? — Inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy, severe malnutrition.

How would you modify fluid resuscitation in a patient with suspected septic shock and concurrent severe malaria? — Give small boluses (10 ml/kg) and reassess; avoid large volumes that precipitate pulmonary oedema.
What are the key components of a head‑to‑toe exam for a patient with suspected TB? — General appearance, lymphadenopathy, chest auscultation, abdominal organomegaly, musculoskeletal tenderness.
Why is point‑of‑care ultrasound valuable when a chest X‑ray is unavailable? — It can detect pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and assess cardiac contractility at bedside.
Explain why a patient with sickle cell disease may have a normal chest X‑ray despite acute chest syndrome. — Early infiltrates may be subtle; rely on clinical signs and oxygen saturation.
ai.title: Head-to-Toe Clinical Assessment
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A systematic bedside approach to evaluate every organ system, linking findings to common tropical diseases and low‑resource constraints. Emphasises pattern recognition, red‑flags and pragmatic investigations.

b: Starts with general appearance, vital signs and mental status
Follows a predictable order to avoid missing findings
sections.p: A head‑to‑toe assessment is a structured physical exam that identifies organ‑specific pathology by inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.

b: Mild: isolated sign, stable vitals
Moderate: multiple systems involved, borderline vitals
Severe: organ failure, shock, altered consciousness
sections.p: Severity is judged by the extent of organ dysfunction and systemic response (e.g., sepsis criteria, WHO danger signs).

b: Infectious: malaria, TB, HIV, hepatitis B
Hematologic: sickle cell disease, severe anemia
Cardiopulmonary: rheumatic heart disease, chronic lung disease
Renal/hepatic: schistosomiasis, hepatitis
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent causes of abnormal findings are infectious (malaria, TB, HIV‑related opportunistic infections), hematologic (sickle cell, anemia), and chronic (rheumatic heart disease, schistosomiasis).

b: General: fever, weight loss, night sweats
Head/neck: lymphadenopathy, oral thrush (HIV)
Chest: tachypnea, wheeze, crackles
Abdomen: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites
Extremities: edema, cyanosis, clubbing
sections.p: Key patterns guide diagnosis: fever with hepatosplenomegaly suggests malaria or TB; pallor with jaundice points to hemolysis; crackles with peripheral edema indicate heart failure.
Select tests that answer the clinical question; when unavailable, rely on bedside clues or point‑of‑care tools.

t.b: Is malaria present? Positive test confirms Plasmodium infection; negative test prompts microscopy or alternative diagnosis.
Is anemia or leukocytosis present? Low Hb indicates anemia; high WBC suggests infection.
Is there pulmonary infiltrate or cardiomegaly? Infiltrate supports pneumonia; enlarged heart suggests heart failure.
Is there protein or blood? Proteinuria may indicate renal disease; hematuria suggests schistosomiasis.
Is there free fluid or organ enlargement? Detects ascites, pleural effusion, enlarged liver/spleen.

b: Altered mental status
Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) or shock
Severe respiratory distress (RR >30, SpO2 <90%)
Rapidly rising creatinine or bilirubin
sections.p: Identify signs that demand urgent intervention.

b: Antimicrobials: artesunate for severe malaria, first‑line anti‑TB regimen, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV
Fluid management: cautious IV crystalloids for shock; avoid overload in heart failure
Oxygen: nasal cannula or simple mask if SpO2 <90%
Transfusion: packed RBCs for Hb <7 g/dL in symptomatic patients
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care tailored to resource limits.

b: Schedule repeat malaria test if fever persists
Monitor hemoglobin weekly in sickle cell
Provide insecticide‑treated nets and health education
sections.p: Re‑examine within 24‑48 h to assess response; educate on vector control, vaccination and adherence to chronic therapy.

b: Sepsis vs. severe malaria – both cause fever, tachycardia, hypotension; malaria has periodic chills and positive rapid test
Heart failure vs. severe anemia – both cause dyspnea; anemia lacks pulmonary crackles and elevated JVP
sections.p: Conditions that mimic similar systemic signs.

b: Negative malaria rapid test in low‑parasitemia – confirm with microscopy
Normal chest X‑ray early in pulmonary TB – rely on clinical suspicion and sputum if possible
sections.p: Laboratory or bedside findings that may be falsely reassuring.
